summary: Coast Guard light at the mouth of Queen Charlotte Strait, first lit in 1907 from a square wooden tower; rebuilt after the 1967 storm and in 2001; staffed today.

structures.note: 43 ft from base to lantern ventilator; square wooden dwelling at one corner; polygonal iron lantern.
Rectangular wooden building, 200 feet northwest of the lighthouse.
Diaphone plant installed in the year to 31 March 1908.
Standing by 1967 (LighthouseFriends); the change is not dated.

structures.type: square steel tower with lantern and skeletal bracing
structures.note: Directory: 10.5 m (35 ft); repaired after the 1967 storm.
Directory summary: round cylindrical steel, white, without lantern. Coast Guard list: square.

staffing.note: Keeper list runs to at least 2024 (LighthouseFriends). Senate 2010 table: two positions, permanent residents.

access.note: Staffed Coast Guard light where keepers live. Reached only by boat. Visitors should not land without the Coast Guard's invitation.

visit.grounds_note: LighthouseFriends: grounds open, tower closed. The Lighthouse Directory: site and tower closed. Lantern, lens and foghorn of the earlier light are displayed at the Campbell River Maritime Heritage Centre.

events.note: Square wooden tower, dwelling and fog alarm building erected by day labour; total cost of the work $21,071.29.
Light and fog alarm ready for service by 31 March 1907.
Diaphone plant installed in the year to 31 March 1908.
February 1967 gale; a large wave struck the island at night (LighthouseFriends).
Accounts differ. LighthouseFriends: fog signal building destroyed, tower only slightly damaged. Directory: station heavily damaged. Encyclopedia preview: completely destroyed.
Cylindrical white tower replaced the tower that survived the 1967 wave.

corrections.why: The Department's 1907 report describes the finished tower and says the light and fog alarm were ready for service. The record's 1908 comes from Wikidata; in the record 1908 matches the diaphone installation, which is a fog signal, not the tower.

The Directory's 'Inactive since 2001' line refers to the historic lantern now displayed at Campbell River, not to the station. The Directory lists the station as active, and the Coast Guard list gives an active light (Fl R 10s).
The present tower is the one lit today and replaced the tower that survived the 1967 wave.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Sources differed on whether the light is still lit. The Coast Guard list gives Fl R 10s as a current light; the Directory lists it active, and LighthouseFriends describes a flashing red light today. It is lit.
1907 is the tower and light (report to 31 March 1907); 1908 is the diaphone fog signal (report to 31 March 1908). Both are right for different parts of the station.
LighthouseFriends says the grounds are open and the tower closed; the Lighthouse Directory says the site and tower are both closed. The story states both and advises that visitors not land.

notes_for_editor: Rich evidence on the 1906 to 1908 construction, from the Marine annual reports in the corpus, and on the keepers and the 1967 storm, from LighthouseFriends. The 1907 entry is the report for the nine months to 31 March 1907 (its fog-alarm sentence is on printed p. 44, scan p. 51). The 1967 damage is disputed: LighthouseFriends says the tower was only slightly damaged; the Directory says the station was heavily damaged and the tower repaired; the paywalled encyclopedia preview says completely destroyed. The story reports the disagreement and does not settle it. The tower shape is also disputed (Directory: square, then round cylindrical; Coast Guard list: square; LighthouseFriends: cylindrical). The Coast Guard's focal height is 24.6 m; the Directory gives a 28 m focal plane. Not reconciled and not in the story. Access: LighthouseFriends says the grounds are open and the tower closed; the Directory says the site and tower are both closed. The story gives both. Keeper names in the Marine keeper tables (for example A. B. Gurney against Pine island) are OCR columns matched by position; the roster uses LighthouseFriends' published list, which agrees for Gurney, and the story does not rely on the table alone. LighthouseFriends is copyrighted: facts restated in our words; one short quotation of a sentence. The 1967 newspaper is cited second-hand through LighthouseFriends; it is not in the local corpus. Shared names across LighthouseFriends lists (Richard Rose, Arthur Ernest Kelly, Ralph W. Emerich) are not linked. Donald McPhee at Pine Island (1913 to 1919) and Donald Bertram McPhee at Lennard Island (1922 to 1929) are not linked: no source ties them. Ralph W. Emerich's two stints overlap in the source and are kept as printed. The Pike baby's death is included briefly from LighthouseFriends; the editor may cut it. The two Brown children are not named, and their ages are not printed in the story. Rex Brown and J. P. Lewis are named only in their keeper role and in the 1967 account.
